paper.title_en: Differentiable collision-model control for multipartite state engineering: reachability, geometry, and preparation cost
paper.abstract_en: We study a differentiable control architecture for multipartite state engineering in which partial-SWAP collisions, a Heisenberg exchange, are interleaved with layers of local phase rotations. Singular collision angles confine the evolution to invariant supports, impose exact fidelity ceilings, and generate an inverse-distance lower bound on the preparation time nearby. Away from them, numerical certificates show that the sampled couplings reach the whole fixed-excitation sector for sector dimensions up to 21, and optimizations reach fidelities above 0.999 for dimensions up to 1716. At generic couplings the number of rounds needed for a given Dicke fidelity, measured by the ratio of independent phase controls to the projective dimension, is nearly independent of the system size, and the quantum Fisher information spectrum is close to that of a random Gaussian Jacobian. Near full SWAP, a slow-time theory, the sharp form of the inverse-distance bound there, predicts microscopic hitting times without fitted parameters: the distance from the singular point sets the clock and its direction selects the effective control geometry. A detuning sweep along two rays shows that the Dicke horizon follows this law up to a detuning of 0.1, where it is two to five times shorter than at a generic coupling in sectors of dimension 70 to 252, while phase-uniform, random-sign, and Haar-random targets are delayed; beyond a detuning of about 0.3 all targets return to the generic cost. The slow-time value for the Dicke target is nearly the same for sector dimensions from 35 to 252. The exchange graph of the effective theory offers an interpretation of this ordering. Counted in two-qubit gates, generic-coupling preparation is costlier than known Dicke circuits; the architecture offers fixed global couplings, local phase rotations as the only control, and no measurement.
